title: Software Engineering: Selenium Automation
description: Master Selenium 4 for real-world browser automation — W3C WebDriver, relative locators, Grid 4, CDP/BiDi integration, and production CI/CD pipelines.

lessons.title: What Selenium 4 Actually Is
lessons.description: Understand the W3C WebDriver standard that powers modern Selenium.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Selenium 4: A Standards-Based Rewrite

Selenium 4 isn't just a version bump — it's built entirely on the **W3C WebDriver protocol**, the same standard browser vendors (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge) implement natively. Earlier Selenium versions used a legacy JSON Wire Protocol that each browser vendor had to translate; W3C WebDriver removed that translation layer entirely, which is why Selenium 4 is markedly more stable across browsers than Selenium 3 was.

### The architecture
```
Your Test Code
      │  W3C WebDriver protocol (HTTP/JSON)
      ▼
WebDriver (ChromeDriver / GeckoDriver / msedgedriver)
      │  native browser automation APIs
      ▼
Real Browser
```

Since this is the same protocol Appium and Playwright's compatibility layers speak, understanding it here transfers directly to other tools — this is the actual lingua franca of browser (and mobile) automation in 2026, not a Selenium-specific quirk.
lessons.starter_code:
// Selenium 4 uses the same protocol natively supported by every major browser —
// no more vendor-specific JSON Wire Protocol translation.

quiz_data.question: Why is Selenium 4 more stable across different browsers than Selenium 3?
options: It only supports Chrome now
It communicates via the W3C WebDriver standard that browsers implement natively, removing a translation layer
It no longer requires a driver executable
It uses a completely different programming language
quiz_data.explanation: Selenium 3 relied on a legacy JSON Wire Protocol that had to be translated per-browser; Selenium 4 speaks the W3C standard directly, which browser vendors implement themselves.

lessons.title: Selenium Manager: No More Manual Driver Downloads
lessons.description: Set up a project without ever touching a driver binary yourself.
lessons.content_markdown:
## The Old Pain

For years, Selenium users manually downloaded `chromedriver`/`geckodriver`, matched it to their exact browser version, and fixed PATH issues whenever the browser auto-updated and broke everything. This was the single biggest source of Selenium setup frustration.

## Selenium Manager (built into Selenium 4.6+)

```java
// Java — no driver path needed at all
WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();
```
```python
# Python — same story
from selenium import webdriver
driver = webdriver.Chrome()
```

Selenium Manager automatically detects your installed browser version, downloads the matching driver, and caches it — completely eliminating the classic "driver version mismatch" error that used to eat hours of setup time.
lessons.starter_code:
from selenium import webdriver

# Selenium Manager handles the driver automatically
driver = webdriver.Chrome()
driver.get('https://example.com')
print(driver.title)
driver.quit()

lessons.title: Your First Test: The WebDriver Session Lifecycle
lessons.description: Understand what actually happens when you create and quit a driver.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Session Lifecycle

```python
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

driver = webdriver.Chrome()          # 1. Start a new browser session
try:
    driver.get('https://example.com') # 2. Navigate
    heading = driver.find_element(By.TAG_NAME, 'h1')
    assert heading.text == 'Example Domain'
finally:
    driver.quit()                     # 3. Always clean up the session
```

### `quit()` vs `close()`
- `driver.close()` closes the **current window/tab** — if it's the last one, the session ends
- `driver.quit()` closes **all windows** and ends the WebDriver session/process entirely

Always use `quit()` in teardown (a `finally` block or pytest fixture), never `close()` — a leaked WebDriver process on a CI runner will eventually exhaust memory across a long test run.
lessons.starter_code:
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

driver = webdriver.Chrome()
try:
    driver.get('https://example.com')
    heading = driver.find_element(By.TAG_NAME, 'h1')
    assert heading.text == 'Example Domain'
finally:
    driver.quit()

quiz_data.question: Why should test teardown always call driver.quit() instead of driver.close()?
options: close() is deprecated and throws an error
quit() ends the entire WebDriver session and closes all windows, preventing leaked browser processes
close() only works in headless mode
There is no difference between them
quiz_data.explanation: close() only closes the current window; quit() terminates the whole session. Using close() in teardown can leak WebDriver processes across a long CI run.

lessons.title: Relative Locators: Selenium 4's Human-Friendly Selectors
lessons.description: Find elements by their visual relationship to each other, not just by attributes.
lessons.content_markdown:
## "Find the field near this label"

Selenium 4 introduced **relative locators**, letting you locate elements the way a human would describe them — relative to another known element — instead of relying purely on IDs, classes, or XPath ancestry.

```python
from selenium.webdriver.support.relative_locator import locate_with
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

email_label = driver.find_element(By.XPATH, "//label[text()='Email']")
email_input = driver.find_element(locate_with(By.TAG_NAME, 'input').below(email_label))

submit_btn = driver.find_element(locate_with(By.TAG_NAME, 'button').near(email_input))
```

Available relations: `.above()`, `.below()`, `.to_left_of()`, `.to_right_of()`, `.near()`.

### When to use them
Great for legacy forms/UIs with no stable IDs or test attributes. **Not** a replacement for `data-testid` attributes when you control the codebase — explicit test IDs are still more reliable and faster to resolve than relative geometry.
lessons.starter_code:
from selenium.webdriver.support.relative_locator import locate_with
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

email_label = driver.find_element(By.XPATH, "//label[text()='Email']")
email_input = driver.find_element(locate_with(By.TAG_NAME, 'input').below(email_label))
email_input.send_keys('qa@zaka.dev')

lessons.title: Explicit Waits vs. the Implicit Wait Trap
lessons.description: Understand why implicit waits are discouraged in modern Selenium.
lessons.content_markdown:
## The Implicit Wait Problem

```python
driver.implicitly_wait(10)  # applies globally to every find_element call
```

This sounds convenient but causes two real problems:
1. **Mixing implicit and explicit waits** causes unpredictable, inconsistent timeouts that are notoriously hard to debug
2. It waits for **presence**, not **actionability** — an element can exist in the DOM while still being invisible, disabled, or covered, causing `ElementNotInteractableException` even after the 'wait' passes

## Explicit Waits (the correct default)

```python
from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWait
from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as EC
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

wait = WebDriverWait(driver, 10)
button = wait.until(EC.element_to_be_clickable((By.ID, 'submit')))
button.click()
```

`expected_conditions` has dozens of built-in conditions (`visibility_of_element_located`, `text_to_be_present_in_element`, `element_to_be_clickable`) — pick the one that actually matches what you're about to do, not just "does it exist."
lessons.starter_code:
from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWait
from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as EC
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

wait = WebDriverWait(driver, 10)
button = wait.until(EC.element_to_be_clickable((By.ID, 'submit')))
button.click()

quiz_data.question: Why is mixing implicit and explicit waits in the same test discouraged?
options: It causes a syntax error
It produces unpredictable, inconsistent effective timeouts that are hard to debug
Implicit waits are removed in Selenium 4
It only affects Firefox
quiz_data.explanation: The two wait mechanisms interact in non-obvious ways when combined, producing effective wait times that don't match either configured value — a well-documented source of Selenium flakiness.

lessons.title: The Actions API: Gestures, Drag-and-Drop & Keyboard
lessons.description: Simulate complex, multi-step user interactions.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Beyond click() and send_keys()

The `ActionChains` API composes low-level mouse/keyboard events into complex gestures:

```python
from selenium.webdriver.common.action_chains import ActionChains
from selenium.webdriver.common.keys import Keys

actions = ActionChains(driver)

# Drag and drop
actions.drag_and_drop(source_element, target_element).perform()

# Hover then click a revealed menu item
actions.move_to_element(menu_trigger).pause(0.3).click(submenu_item).perform()

# Keyboard shortcut (Ctrl+A, then type)
actions.key_down(Keys.CONTROL).send_keys('a').key_up(Keys.CONTROL).send_keys('replacement text').perform()
```

Each call queues an action; nothing happens until `.perform()` executes the whole sequence — this matters because it lets you build a precise, deliberate interaction script instead of hoping individual clicks land in the right order.
lessons.starter_code:
from selenium.webdriver.common.action_chains import ActionChains

actions = ActionChains(driver)
actions.drag_and_drop(source_element, target_element).perform()

lessons.title: Handling Alerts, Frames & Multiple Windows
lessons.description: Navigate the browser contexts that trip up most beginners.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Native Alerts
```python
alert = driver.switch_to.alert
print(alert.text)
alert.accept()   # or alert.dismiss()
```

## iframes
```python
driver.switch_to.frame('payment-frame')
driver.find_element(By.ID, 'card-number').send_keys('4242424242424242')
driver.switch_to.default_content()  # back to the main page
```

## Multiple Windows/Tabs
```python
original_window = driver.current_window_handle
driver.find_element(By.LINK_TEXT, 'Open in new tab').click()

for handle in driver.window_handles:
    if handle != original_window:
        driver.switch_to.window(handle)
        break

# ... interact with the new tab ...
driver.close()
driver.switch_to.window(original_window)
```

Forgetting to switch back to `default_content()` or the original window is one of the most common causes of "element not found" errors right after a frame/tab interaction — Selenium keeps looking in whatever context you last switched to.
lessons.starter_code:
original_window = driver.current_window_handle
driver.find_element(By.LINK_TEXT, 'Open in new tab').click()

for handle in driver.window_handles:
    if handle != original_window:
        driver.switch_to.window(handle)
        break

driver.close()
driver.switch_to.window(original_window)

quiz_data.question: What is a common cause of 'element not found' errors right after interacting with an iframe?
options: The iframe was deleted
Forgetting to call driver.switch_to.default_content() to return to the main page context
iframes are not supported in Selenium 4
The element was never visible
quiz_data.explanation: Selenium continues searching within whatever frame context you last switched into; forgetting to switch back to default_content() means subsequent find_element calls look in the wrong document.

lessons.title: Page Object Model, Done Right
lessons.description: Structure a test suite that survives real-world UI changes.
lessons.content_markdown:
## The Pattern

```python
class LoginPage:
    def __init__(self, driver):
        self.driver = driver
        self.email_input = (By.ID, 'email')
        self.password_input = (By.ID, 'password')
        self.submit_button = (By.ID, 'submit')

    def load(self):
        self.driver.get('https://app.example.com/login')

    def login(self, email, password):
        self.driver.find_element(*self.email_input).send_keys(email)
        self.driver.find_element(*self.password_input).send_keys(password)
        self.driver.find_element(*self.submit_button).click()
```

Tests then read like plain English and never reference raw selectors:
```python
def test_valid_login(driver):
    login_page = LoginPage(driver)
    login_page.load()
    login_page.login('qa@zaka.dev', 'Secure123!')
    assert 'dashboard' in driver.current_url
```

When the login form's HTML changes, you update `LoginPage` in exactly one place — every test that logs in benefits automatically.

lessons.title: Data-Driven Testing with Pytest Parametrization
lessons.description: Run the same test logic against many inputs without copy-pasting.
lessons.content_markdown:
## `@pytest.mark.parametrize`

```python
import pytest

@pytest.mark.parametrize('email,password,expected_error', [
    ('', 'Secure123!', 'Email is required'),
    ('bad-email', 'Secure123!', 'Enter a valid email'),
    ('qa@zaka.dev', '', 'Password is required'),
])
def test_login_validation(driver, email, password, expected_error):
    login_page = LoginPage(driver)
    login_page.load()
    login_page.login(email, password)
    error = driver.find_element(By.CLASS_NAME, 'error-message')
    assert expected_error in error.text
```

This generates three independent test cases from one function — each shows up separately in your test report, and a failure in one doesn't hide failures in the others (unlike a hand-rolled `for` loop inside a single test).
lessons.starter_code:
import pytest

@pytest.mark.parametrize('email,password,expected_error', [
    ('', 'Secure123!', 'Email is required'),
    ('bad-email', 'Secure123!', 'Enter a valid email'),
])
def test_login_validation(driver, email, password, expected_error):
    login_page = LoginPage(driver)
    login_page.load()
    login_page.login(email, password)
    error = driver.find_element(By.CLASS_NAME, 'error-message')
    assert expected_error in error.text

quiz_data.question: Why is @pytest.mark.parametrize preferred over a manual for-loop inside one test function?
options: It runs faster
Each parameter set becomes its own independent, separately-reported test case, so one failure doesn't mask others
It's the only way to use variables in pytest
It automatically fixes failing assertions
quiz_data.explanation: Parametrization generates distinct test cases visible individually in reports; a for-loop inside one test stops at the first failed assertion and hides results for remaining inputs.

lessons.title: Custom Wait Conditions & Fluent Waits
lessons.description: Write your own expected_condition when the built-ins don't fit.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Beyond the Built-Ins

Sometimes no built-in `expected_condition` matches what you need. Write your own as a callable:

```python
class element_has_css_class:
    def __init__(self, locator, css_class):
        self.locator = locator
        self.css_class = css_class

    def __call__(self, driver):
        element = driver.find_element(*self.locator)
        return self.css_class in element.get_attribute('class')

wait.until(element_has_css_class((By.ID, 'save-button'), 'is-saved'))
```

## Fluent Wait

A `WebDriverWait` with custom polling frequency and ignored exceptions:
```python
from selenium.common.exceptions import NoSuchElementException

fluent_wait = WebDriverWait(
    driver, timeout=15, poll_frequency=0.5,
    ignored_exceptions=[NoSuchElementException]
)
fluent_wait.until(lambda d: d.find_element(By.ID, 'result').is_displayed())
```

Use a custom polling interval when the default 500ms is either too slow (fast-updating UI) or wastefully frequent (an operation you know takes several seconds).

lessons.title: Selenium Grid 4 Architecture
lessons.description: Understand the distributed model that replaced the old Hub/Node setup.
lessons.content_markdown:
## From Hub/Node to Fully Distributed

Selenium Grid 4 was rearchitected around four independent components that can run standalone or distributed: the **Router**, **Distributor**, **Session Map**, and **Node**. In practice, most teams use Grid in one of two modes:

- **Standalone**: everything in one process — fine for local testing
- **Fully distributed**: components scaled independently across machines — used for real CI fleets

```bash
# Standalone mode (single command, good for local/small CI)
java -jar selenium-server-4.jar standalone
```

Tests connect to the Grid exactly the same way regardless of mode — you just change the `command_executor` URL:
```python
from selenium.webdriver.common.desired_capabilities import DesiredCapabilities

driver = webdriver.Remote(
    command_executor='http://localhost:4444/wd/hub',
    options=webdriver.ChromeOptions()
)
```
lessons.starter_code:
driver = webdriver.Remote(
    command_executor='http://localhost:4444/wd/hub',
    options=webdriver.ChromeOptions()
)

lessons.title: Running Grid via Docker Compose
lessons.description: Stand up a real multi-browser Grid without installing anything locally.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Docker-Based Grid

Selenium publishes official Docker images for exactly this — no local Java/browser driver installation needed at all.

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  selenium-hub:
    image: selenium/hub:4.20
    ports: ['4442:4442', '4443:4443', '4444:4444']

  chrome:
    image: selenium/node-chrome:4.20
    depends_on: [selenium-hub]
    environment:
      - SE_EVENT_BUS_HOST=selenium-hub
      - SE_EVENT_BUS_PUBLISH_PORT=4442
      - SE_EVENT_BUS_SUBSCRIBE_PORT=4443

  firefox:
    image: selenium/node-firefox:4.20
    depends_on: [selenium-hub]
    environment:
      - SE_EVENT_BUS_HOST=selenium-hub
      - SE_EVENT_BUS_PUBLISH_PORT=4442
      - SE_EVENT_BUS_SUBSCRIBE_PORT=4443
```

```bash
docker compose up -d
# Grid console: http://localhost:4444/ui
```

This is the most common way real teams run cross-browser Grid today — reproducible, disposable, and identical between a developer's laptop and CI.
lessons.starter_code:
# docker-compose.yml (simplified)
# services:
#   selenium-hub:
#     image: selenium/hub:4.20
#   chrome:
#     image: selenium/node-chrome:4.20
#     depends_on: [selenium-hub]

# docker compose up -d

quiz_data.question: What is the main advantage of running Selenium Grid via Docker Compose?
options: It's the only way to use more than one browser
It gives a reproducible, disposable Grid setup that's identical across a developer's machine and CI
It makes tests run without any code changes
It removes the need for WebDriver entirely
quiz_data.explanation: Docker images bundle the exact browser + driver versions, so the Grid environment is consistent everywhere it runs — a major source of 'works on my machine' Grid issues is eliminated.

lessons.title: Cloud Execution: BrowserStack & Sauce Labs
lessons.description: Scale beyond your own infrastructure using real device/browser clouds.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Pointing at a Cloud Grid

Cloud providers expose a Selenium-compatible Grid endpoint — your test code barely changes, only the capabilities and remote URL:

```python
import os

options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
options.set_capability('bstack:options', {
    'os': 'Windows', 'osVersion': '11',
    'browserVersion': 'latest',
    'userName': os.environ['BROWSERSTACK_USERNAME'],
    'accessKey': os.environ['BROWSERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY'],
})

driver = webdriver.Remote(
    command_executor='https://hub-cloud.browserstack.com/wd/hub',
    options=options
)
```

This is the same pattern used across the industry: local Grid for fast feedback during development, cloud Grid for the full real-device/browser matrix in CI before a release.

lessons.title: Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) Integration
lessons.description: Intercept network traffic and capture console logs directly from Selenium.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Beyond WebDriver: CDP Access

Selenium 4 exposes Chromium's DevTools Protocol directly, letting you do things plain WebDriver never could:

```python
from selenium.webdriver.common.bidi.network import Network

driver = webdriver.Chrome()
devtools = driver.execute_cdp_cmd

# Simulate offline network
driver.execute_cdp_cmd('Network.enable', {})
driver.execute_cdp_cmd('Network.emulateNetworkConditions', {
    'offline': True, 'latency': 0, 'downloadThroughput': 0, 'uploadThroughput': 0
})

# Capture console messages
driver.execute_cdp_cmd('Runtime.enable', {})
logs = driver.get_log('browser')
```

This unlocks network condition simulation, console log capture, and performance metrics — capabilities that used to require a separate proxy tool (like BrowserMob Proxy) bolted onto Selenium.

lessons.title: BiDi Protocol: The Future Beyond CDP
lessons.description: Understand where Selenium's browser-communication model is heading.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Why BiDi Matters

CDP integration is powerful but **Chromium-specific** — it doesn't work the same way in Firefox or Safari. The **WebDriver BiDi** (bi-directional) protocol is the W3C's cross-browser answer: a standardized way to get the same network interception, console log access, and real-time event streaming CDP offers, but working identically across all major browsers.

```python
# BiDi support is landing incrementally across Selenium bindings
with driver.bidi_connection() as session:
    network = Network(driver)
    # subscribe to network events across ANY browser, not just Chromium
```

As of 2026, BiDi support varies by language binding and browser — check current compatibility before depending on it in production, but understand it's the direction the entire ecosystem (Selenium, Playwright, and browser vendors) is converging on.
lessons.starter_code:
# BiDi usage pattern (support varies by binding/browser — check current docs)
# with driver.bidi_connection() as session:
#     network = Network(driver)
#     ...

quiz_data.question: Why is the WebDriver BiDi protocol significant compared to CDP-based integration?
options: It's faster than CDP in every case
It's a W3C cross-browser standard, unlike CDP which is Chromium-specific
It replaces the need for a browser driver
It only works in headless mode
quiz_data.explanation: CDP only works with Chromium-based browsers; BiDi is being standardized across all major browsers, meaning the same interception/logging capabilities work consistently everywhere.

lessons.title: Full-Page & Element Screenshots
lessons.description: Capture visual evidence precisely, using Selenium 4's improved API.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Element-Level Screenshots

```python
# Selenium 4: screenshot a single element, not just the viewport
element = driver.find_element(By.ID, 'pricing-card')
element.screenshot('pricing-card.png')
```

## Full-Page Screenshots

Standard `driver.save_screenshot()` only captures the visible viewport. For a true full-page capture, combine with CDP:
```python
result = driver.execute_cdp_cmd('Page.captureScreenshot', {'captureBeyondViewport': True})
import base64
with open('full-page.png', 'wb') as f:
    f.write(base64.b64decode(result['data']))
```

Element-level and full-page screenshots are especially useful for **failure diagnostics** — attach them automatically in a pytest fixture's teardown so every failed test leaves visual evidence in your CI artifacts.
lessons.starter_code:
element = driver.find_element(By.ID, 'pricing-card')
element.screenshot('pricing-card.png')

lessons.title: Headless Execution & CI Configuration
lessons.description: Run your Selenium suite reliably inside GitHub Actions.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Headless Chrome in CI

```python
options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
options.add_argument('--headless=new')
options.add_argument('--no-sandbox')
options.add_argument('--disable-dev-shm-usage')
driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
```

The last two flags matter specifically in containerized CI: `--no-sandbox` avoids a common Docker permission failure, and `--disable-dev-shm-usage` prevents Chrome from crashing when `/dev/shm` is too small (the default in many CI containers).

## GitHub Actions Workflow
```yaml
name: Selenium Tests
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: '3.12' }
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest --html=report.html
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with: { name: test-report, path: report.html }
```
lessons.starter_code:
options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
options.add_argument('--headless=new')
options.add_argument('--no-sandbox')
options.add_argument('--disable-dev-shm-usage')
driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)

lessons.title: Diagnosing Flaky Tests
lessons.description: Systematically find the real cause instead of just adding retries.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Retries Hide Problems, They Don't Fix Them

A `pytest-rerunfailures` retry is a reasonable safety net, but treating it as the primary fix for flakiness just delays the same failure. Common real causes, in order of frequency:

1. **Race conditions** — clicking before an async UI update finishes (fix: proper explicit waits, not more retries)
2. **Shared test state** — tests that depend on execution order or leftover data from a previous test
3. **Animation timing** — clicking a button mid-transition
4. **Environment differences** — CI runs headless/smaller viewport than local, changing layout

### A practical debugging checklist
```python
@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def screenshot_on_failure(request, driver):
    yield
    if request.node.rep_call.failed:
        driver.save_screenshot(f'failures/{request.node.name}.png')
```
Capture screenshots (and ideally the page source) automatically on failure — guessing at flaky failures without evidence wastes far more time than the instrumentation costs.

quiz_data.question: What is the main risk of using test retries as the primary strategy for handling flaky tests?
options: Retries are not supported in pytest
It masks the real underlying cause (race conditions, shared state, timing) instead of fixing it
Retries always make tests slower with no benefit
It's impossible to configure retries in CI
quiz_data.explanation: Retries can be a reasonable safety net, but relying on them alone means the actual root cause of flakiness (often a real race condition or bug) never gets diagnosed or fixed.

lessons.title: Capstone: E2E Suite for an E-Commerce Site
lessons.description: Combine everything into one production-shaped test suite.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Capstone Brief

Build a suite covering:

1. **Page Object Model** for Login, Product Search, and Checkout pages
2. **Relative locators** for a legacy-style product filter sidebar with no test IDs
3. **Explicit waits** throughout — no implicit waits
4. **Parametrized data-driven tests** for search queries and checkout validation errors
5. **CI integration** — headless Chrome, screenshot-on-failure, HTML report artifact

```python
class TestCheckoutFlow:
    def test_add_to_cart_and_checkout(self, driver):
        search_page = SearchPage(driver)
        search_page.load()
        search_page.search('mechanical keyboard')
        search_page.add_first_result_to_cart()

        cart_page = CartPage(driver)
        cart_page.load()
        assert cart_page.item_count() == 1

        checkout_page = cart_page.proceed_to_checkout()
        checkout_page.fill_shipping_info(name='Test User', address='123 Main St')
        checkout_page.submit_order()

        assert 'Order confirmed' in driver.page_source
```

This mirrors what a real QA engineer builds day-to-day: a maintainable page-object suite, data-driven validation coverage, and CI wired to surface failures with evidence — not a one-off script.
lessons.starter_code:
class TestCheckoutFlow:
    def test_add_to_cart_and_checkout(self, driver):
        search_page = SearchPage(driver)
        search_page.load()
        search_page.search('mechanical keyboard')
        search_page.add_first_result_to_cart()

        cart_page = CartPage(driver)
        cart_page.load()
        assert cart_page.item_count() == 1

        checkout_page = cart_page.proceed_to_checkout()
        checkout_page.fill_shipping_info(name='Test User', address='123 Main St')
        checkout_page.submit_order()

        assert 'Order confirmed' in driver.page_source

lessons.title: Capstone Knowledge Check
lessons.description: Final review covering the full course.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Final Review

Before moving on, make sure you can confidently answer:

- Why does Selenium 4's W3C-native protocol reduce cross-browser flakiness compared to Selenium 3?
- When are relative locators the right tool, and when is a `data-testid` still better?
- Why is mixing implicit and explicit waits dangerous?
- What's the actual difference Docker-based Grid makes versus a manually installed one?
- Why should retries never be your only strategy for flaky tests?

If these all feel solid, you're ready to own a real Selenium automation strategy end-to-end — not just write individual scripts, but architect a suite that survives contact with a real, evolving product.
